title: The troop train and Colonel Ned Gardine of the 372nd Infantry
summary: The long troop train trip to Kentucky; the all-Black 372nd under Colonel Gardine, a Howard athlete and lawyer, and a pointed protocol moment on arrival.

blocks.x: So we were at Breckenridge, all the same, and I'll tell you this, a little side story. Of course when the regiment got on this troop train, that was a good experience too, this troop train. I didn't like it, but I liked the

experience of it. We stayed on this troop train about two or three days, going from New York to Kentucky. Now, the way this train, troop train, went to Kentucky, we started out from New York, we went west. Then we went north. We went around through North Dakota. That's the Army for you. We carried all the cooks, everything. The cooks were on the train cooking. The Army cooks, you know. Troop train. It wasn't a pullman car. It was a troop train. It was made for this purpose, to carry troops. So we wound around, and we used to get off the train and line up and exercise. Real maneuver. So we got to -- now, when the troop train got to Breckenridge, of course the Commander of the camp was a white officer, naturally, and he was a Lieutenant Colonel, which is one step below our Colonel, who was a full Colonel. So naturally the way they do it, you know, protocol, whatever, he stepped off the train and they saluted each other and shook hands and talked. And went about, you know, the business of reporting and whatever. And the next day this white Colonel, he was a full Colonel, the next day. Can you imagine? Yeah. He probably was a regular Army man. Well, he had to be to be a Colonel at that point. And he was probably in the Army 40 years, and all of a sudden he gets promoted to be on even terms with our Colonel. And our Colonel was Colonel Ned Gardine , who was a Howard man, and during his college career he was an athlete. He was national broad jump
champion. And he was also a lawyer. And when the -- after the war he became a Judge. So that was his background, and that was a -- so the regiment was under very good command, I would say.
